segments.text: Hello and welcome to this week's Health Report with me, Norman Swan. Today, important consumer advice for men heading for a prostate biopsy.
Barbaric is what one urologist calls the commonest technique for doing this. Keep your legs crossed till then.
Canada's first female Aboriginal psychiatrist is on the programme. Canadian First Nations like ours experienced stolen generations, in their case, through residential schools.
But unlike Australia, Canada's had a Truth and Reconciliation Commission. Find out more later.
how post-traumatic stress disorder can be as much a set of physical problems as psychological,
and national shortages of life-saving drugs.
Last week, a group of infectious disease physicians called for a national strategy
to deal with drug shortages in Australia.
This is an under-the-radar issue with several powerful antibiotics in short supply nationally,
with some states being held hostage to higher prices from suppliers
or substitution for medications which are not so fit for purpose.
Someone who's documented the issue is Professor Alan Cheng in the Department of Infectious Diseases
at Alfred Health, and he's in our Melbourne studio. Welcome, Alan.
Good afternoon.
What drugs are we talking about here?
Oh, look, there's been quite a range of them over the last couple of years.
So the most recent have been vancomycin and daptomycin, which are used for staph infections,
golden staph infections.
We've had shortages of metronidazole, acyclovir, penicillin, the hep B vaccine now.
So it really is quite a range of different things.
Yes, yes.
I think one of the manufacturers has had a temporary stop to supply of one of the vaccines.
So just to translate that for people who've never heard of these drugs,
so vancomycin is one of the antibiotics of last resort for people who've got serious infection.
Metronidazole treats fungal infections, acyclovir, serious herpes infections.
I mean, these are not trivial drugs.
Exactly.
And I think what it really goes to is that these are life-saving drugs and we really need to get them quickly when we do need them.
So we've actually run out of them at times in Australia?
I think it's a variable.
I think some hospitals have had some small stockpiles left.
So often when we've run out at our hospital, we've just done a ring around and found a bit of a supply elsewhere.
Sometimes the drug distributor holds a little bit back
and you give them a call and they'll release you a bit of stock
if you beg and plead a bit.
And sometimes we have run out completely
and we've just had to go to something else
or to another overseas supplier.
And you've done a survey of infectious disease physicians
who reckons half the time patients come to some harm
or at least they don't benefit as much as they should.
Yeah, I think there's three major impacts on patients.
The lack of availability is really like
as if the bug was resistant.
You don't have that treatment option for that infection.
And sometimes that's really important.
So penicillin for syphilis is really the only treatment.
All the others are sort of second best.
So when we had problems with penicillin supply,
we really had to conserve whatever penicillin we had
for syphilis specifically.
The second problem is that sometimes the options are more toxic.
So daptomycin is an example of that,
where when we ran out of that,
we had to move to a different antibiotic called linezolid,
which you can't really use for more than two weeks,
so it causes bone marrow toxicity and nerve damage.
And then the third problem is that sometimes we have to go to broader spectrum antibiotics.
So when we ran out of penicillin, the option for that is often keftriaxone.
That's a broad spectrum antibiotic that can generate antibiotic-resistant organisms in itself,
so that has an impact on what we call antibiotic stewardship programs.
And I've also seen some data where when you go to another manufacturer, they charge you 10 times as much, you know, where a drug that might cost, you know, $4,000 per course costs $40,000.
I mean, it's just extraordinary.
Yeah.
So I guess there's two aspects to the cost.
There's the procurement cost, which obviously can be significant.
And often there are small manufacturers or small distributors that step in, but also the cost of just the pharmacist having to source these.
So why do these shortages occur?
It's sounding like a third world nation.
I would probably emphasize that this is sort of a little bit of a first world problem.
So in third world countries, they really don't have these drugs at all.
And that's a major problem.
Fair enough.
But why have we got a problem?
So I'm not really sure.
I think the main reason is that there are not many suppliers and particularly for antibiotics
that have been generic for a long time and manufacturers don't make a lot of profit from
them.
They may not invest in sort of state-of-the-art factories.
And so if a factory goes down, that can sort of have ripple effects.
I think it also speaks to that we have really long supply chains now.
So one manufacturer will get it from another manufacturer who will get it from somewhere else.
And then there may not be very good communication up the chain when there is a problem at a factory.
And 50% of the time it's a quality issue and the factory's taken offline
and suddenly you discover that you're not getting the drug anymore.
Yeah, exactly.
And even where there might be an alternative manufacturer,
they can't ramp up production very quickly.
So there's still a shortage.
And it's not just antibiotics, chemotherapy, painkillers, other things as well.
Oh, yes, absolutely.
So there's a sort of category of life-saving drugs.
And so infrequently used vaccines, BCG, for example.
So when I last covered this, I was told,
there, there, Sonny, don't you worry about it.
The Therapeutic Goods Administration has got this in hand.
there's not much evidence of drug shortages in Australia.
Well, what you're telling me is that's not true.
Yeah, there are some provisions under the Therapeutic Goods Act
to ensure continued supply, but they're really, on paper,
they look good, but they don't give us the access
when we really need them.
And for antibiotics, that's, you know,
you've got the patient in front of you,
you need to treat them in, you know, hours.
So what do we need to do?
So I think we really need to recognise
that these are life-saving drugs
and that we need to build them into the hospital procurement contracts
to say that we need to at least warning and if not continued supply.
I think we need a list of what are these drugs
and we need to be able to communicate between hospitals to say,
this hospital is holding some
or these hospitals can be designated to hold a stockpile.
I mean, I saw a graph of yours of Melbourne hospitals
and there's quite a lot that have only got seven to ten days supply.
Yeah, so if you put the request out to a distributor,
often it takes seven to 10 days to get a drug in.
And when we did that survey of Melbourne hospitals,
we sort of realised that we're actually all holding the same drug
and some of the drugs that we really did want,
none of the hospitals were holding.
Terrifying.
And I assume this is not just a Victorian problem.
No, it would be certainly a national problem.
So we need action.
We do, and I think it just needs to be coordinated
so that we're sort of all on the same page and can do it most efficiently.
Mildly scary.
Alan, thanks for joining us.
No worries.
Thank you very much.
Professor Alan Chang is in the Department of Infectious Diseases at Alfred Health
and he's also in the School of Public Health and Preventive Medicine at Monash University.
You're listening to The Health Report here on RN, ABC News Radio and CBC Radio across Canada.
I'm Norman Swan.
Now, what could be a more purely psychological problem than post-traumatic stress disorder
where a proportion of people who've experienced traumatic events are left with disabling anxiety, flashbacks, depression,
behavioural issues and sometimes drug and alcohol use.
PTSD can affect up to 20% of Australian military personnel who've seen active duty,
but it also occurs to non-military personnel after traumatic events.
Well, a study in today's edition of the Medical Journal of Australia has findings which suggest that PTSD is not just a psychological condition.
The study concludes that PTSD affects the whole body
and should be considered what's called a systemic disorder,
like diabetes, for example, which involves multiple organs.
And it could help to explain why PTSD has been so hard to treat.
Professor Daryl Crawford is Director of Research
at the Gallipoli Medical Research Foundation at the University of Queensland
and is in our Brisbane studio.
Welcome to The Health Report.
Good afternoon, Norman.
So tell us about this study that you did.
Well, this is a very rigorous study of the nature and prevalence of physical comorbidities in patients with PTSD.
And when you say comorbidities, these are problems which coincide or live in the, you know, that go along with the other problem, the other condition, when in this case it's PTSD.
That's correct.
And they were determined by a self-reporting questionnaire that our subjects completed,
as well as a battery of advanced non-invasive diagnostic tests that help us to define the extent and nature of these problems.
And these were Vietnam veterans?
These were Vietnam veterans? That's correct, yes.
So they're not young anymore?
No, they're not.
And as you know, these are veterans with trauma exposure almost 50 years ago.
So I think that is one of the interesting things here, that these symptoms and the health effects of this trauma exposure continues for decades after the initial exposure.
So you compared them to people who experienced trauma but didn't have PTSD.
That's correct.
And you were looking at the differences between the two groups.
Yes. So we had 105 patients who were confirmed by a series of tests to have PTSD and 106 who
were negative. So we had quite a large sample size. And we investigated these patients,
as I said, with a variety of diagnostic tests and self-reporting questionnaires.
So what did you find?
We found some interesting facts. I mean, I guess the highlight facts are that
the patients with PTSD had a four times higher risk of previous acute myocardial infarction.
Heart attack?
Heart attack.
They had a two-fold increase in sleep disturbances and particularly obstructive sleep apnea and
restless legs.
A two-fold increase in peptic ulcer disease and irritable bowel syndrome and constipation.
There were a number of lifestyle factors, I think, that contributed to diseases that
are really coping responses. And so, for instance, we found that the patients with PTSD had slightly
higher body mass indexes. They consumed more cigarettes and had a higher lifetime alcohol
consumption. Clearly, these sort of factors impacted on some of the adverse outcomes of
some of the diagnostic tests that we employed. But you removed those factors as well. I mean,
You subtracted those factors from it and you still found physical symptoms and indeed serious outcomes independent of the fact that they smoked and maybe ate too much unhealthy food.

Yes, I think this is actually a real strength of the study was trying to tease out those factors which were related to lifestyle factors or to depression and anxiety, which are obviously often part and parcel of the PTSD complex.
But we were left with some variables or some health outcomes that were unexplained by either lifestyle factors or by anxiety or depression.
And were they particular or was it just part of that general grouping of heart disease?
No, no, they're quite particular.
Such as?
So such as peptic ulcer disease, irritable bowel syndrome, constipation, hearing loss, and then some changes in respiratory measurements, as well as some biochemical tests.
So you're making a call here that this should be called a systemic disorder.
In other words, a disorder that affects the whole body, not just the mind.
But of course, we've got a situation here where we've grown up with this Cartesian.
You know, Descartes said the mind and the body were split.
But in fact, the mind and body are one.
Are we talking about a complex interaction between what goes on in the brain and the rest of the body?
Or how do you explain what's going on?
Because it's not just a secondary phenomenon to stress and lifestyle problems as a result.
Yes, I think that we have to regard this as a condition which has a number of physical comorbidities that in their own right affect the patient's overall health.
and the outcomes which remain unexplained
by the process of this study,
there still are potential explanations
that are not related to neurochemical transmission
or other factors or stress responses.
What do you mean?
Well, I think if you look at, say, peptic ulcer disease,
it's possible that there may have been for some reason
rather a higher exposure to helicobacter in those patients with PTSD.
I think that...
And I think there's a research project that has gone on
looking at more recent Middle Eastern campaigns
which suggest the more desert environment,
the more dirty the environment that you've been exposed to,
the more physical problems you get along with the PTSD.
Yes, and so I think we do have to try to tease out some of these factors.
But I think that there is an increasing shift towards the idea, as you say, of trying to link physical symptoms, which we all feel in certain times of stress with central neurological...
So does the feedback loop go the other way, that the physical symptoms make the psychological problem worse?
I think it probably does.
I think that these factors that we've identified would continue to impact adversely on the health of the veteran with PTSD.
So what does it mean for treatment? Because it's not just veterans we're talking about here.

No, I know. I think that it's not just Vietnam veterans either. I think that, to me, I think that the pointy end of this really is that we have to continue to address the health risk behaviours in Vietnam veterans and also in younger veterans.
I think it is reasonable to assume that if we neglect our younger veterans, that the same health outcomes that we've seen in the Vietnam veterans will apply to the younger veterans.
I think that it should alert health care providers to the underlying diagnosis of PTSD when patients with a history of trauma exposure present with this sort of cluster of physical symptoms.
So keep your eyes open and your attitudes in a box and look at the whole person.
Yeah, I think so.
Luke, thank you very much, Daryl, for coming on the program.
Thank you very much.
Daryl Crawford is Director of Research at the Gallipoli Medical Research Foundation at the University of Queensland.
Many men, when they have a PSA blood test to see if they may be at higher risk of prostate cancer, are sent off for a prostate biopsy.
Most of them will have a biopsy performed through the rectum.
A leading Melbourne urologist argues that a transrectal prostate biopsy in the modern era is barbaric, dangerous and irresponsible.
And the same urologist has evidence of a better way to do the procedure.
He's Associate Professor Jeremy Grumet at Alfred Health and Monash University.
Strong words, Jeremy?
Yeah, hi Norman. I really just use those words to catch your attention.
Oh, you've got it.
So that's good.
Um, but look, yeah, I suppose, uh, when you know that there's an alternative available
that's safer, um, it does shift your perspective a fair bit on.
So what's the safety issue?
Okay.
So normally, uh, as you mentioned, when you, when you do a prostate biopsy, you are going
through the rectum.
The safety issue therefore is that you're passing biopsy needles, uh, through the rectal
wall.
And of course the rectum's whole job is to store feces.
So it makes it extremely difficult not to introduce bacteria into the prostate.
And the prostate's normally a sterile organ with a very good blood supply.
So the problem with that, of course, is that you can then create a severe infection, which
is otherwise known as septicemia or infection in the bloodstream.
Now, we try and counter that with some fairly high-powered broad-spectrum antibiotics prophylactically.
But what we're finding around the world is that those same antibiotics are starting to lose their effect.

And the reason for that is that the normal rectal flora, which is the normal rectal bacteria in people going about their daily business, which are not causing any problems, are becoming more resistant as time goes on to the usual antibiotics that we use.
So you've got a combination of introducing these organisms and the antibiotic cover that you give being less effective or not effective at all.
Correct. And so you can avoid the entire issue by simply passing the biopsy needles through the skin instead of through the rectum.
So you're not dealing with rectal flora at all.
You're just dealing with what we call skin commensals, which are the normal bacteria, the good bacteria that live on the skin.
and they're very easy to get rid of just by typical surgical preparation
with either, you know, betadine or chlorhexidine, just typical disinfectants.
So where is this skin, Jeremy?
The skin?
As I uncross my legs again.
The skin, yeah, well, it's a very sensitive part of the body.
It's the perineum.
So in men, it's between the scrotum and the anus.
And it might sound like not the cleanest part of your body,
but in fact, it's really no different,
particularly once the betadine swabs have been over it to any other part of the skin.
So rusted on neurologists who love doing the transrectal biopsy say,
oh, it's terrific.
You can feel it and you can get to all the different parts of the prostate
and you can do an MRI scan, which really makes it more accurate.
Whereas, you know, it's a pig in a poke, so to speak,
when you're doing it with a transperineally.
No, I don't think that's true, actually.
I would argue the opposite.
I think transperineal biopsy enables you to be very accurate with your MRI targeting.
And that's a whole other issue in terms of the use of MRI prior to biopsy to increase accuracy.
But when you do it via the perineum, you tend to use it with a stabilizing device,
which enables you to perform very accurate biopsies.
And you can direct your needles exactly where you want them to go.
So accuracy is not an issue at all.
So you pick up the tissue if it's going to be there?
Yeah, you almost always do.
And you certainly do.
The other thing is, of course, because you're going through the skin,
you can really take many more biopsies if you feel that's necessary
than what you might be comfortable with going through the rectum.
So you've got a series now, I think, of 1,500 patients
where you've done transperineal biopsies?
Yeah, that's right.
We've certainly published on nearly 1,200 consecutive transperineal biopsies.
And we've got a rate of sepsis of zero.
And the really important point about this, in addition to that, which is obviously, I
mean, obviously we're providing safe care for our patients in that regard.
But on top of that, the last 60% of that cohort only required a single shot of a very basic
antibiotic called kefazolin, which is a first generation keflosporin.
And what that means is that it's just your standard sort of basic antibiotic.
It's nothing.
It's not a big gun antibiotic.
And so the point about that is that we're also avoiding promotion of resistant bacteria by not using it.
How can you get away with it?
If you're telling me that you've got a greater incidence of resistant bacteria, how are you getting away with a basic antibiotic?
Because we're not going through the rectum.
So rectal flora becomes a non-issue completely.
All right.
So you're only doing it for you.
So we're just going through the skin.
And I want to point out that this is a good news story in Australia because this isn't just our group that's performing transperineal biopsy by any means.
This is right across the country and into New Zealand as well.
We did a recent survey of urologists across both countries and we found, in fact, we did the survey twice.
We did it in 2012 and then again last year.
And we found that the rate of urologists doing transperineal biopsy went from one third to two thirds.
So Australia is really leading the world in this area in prostate cancer diagnosis.
It's likely that your favourite urologist is doing this technique.
Does it take a while to learn how to do it?
Yeah, it does, but not really any longer than how to learn how to do a transrectal biopsy,
which we all learn to do as trainees.
So I think one of the rate-limiting steps has been having access to the equipment.
And so still there are centres out there which don't have access to the equipment.
And the other issue that is a real issue, and certainly faced in particular overseas,
is that when you do a transperineal biopsy,
the vast majority of the time
you're doing it under a general anaesthetic.
And that means you've got to take up
operating theater time.
So the cost is higher.
Well, that's right.
There's going to be a higher cost.
However, if you then compare that
to the cost of avoiding sepsis
and sepsis sometimes involves
admissions to the intensive care unit.
But I think you find that it costs 4 million bucks
over five years that they offer it.
Yeah, it's high.
And so if you can avoid that cost of sepsis,
well then you may well be saving money and also saving lives.
So there you are.
Uncross your legs and ask for a transperineal biopsy if you need it.
Jeremy, thanks very much for joining us.
No worries, Norman.
Thank you.
Jeremy Grumet of Alfred Health.
And we included links to a number of Jeremy's research papers on the Health Reports website.
In a history of extraordinary trauma since first contact,
Probably the most traumatic for Australian Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people has been what's called the Stolen Generations,
where Aboriginal children were forcibly and sometimes brutally taken from their families.
Well, Canada has also had its Stolen Generations through residential schools.
But what's different about Canada is that they had a Truth and Reconciliation Commission to confront that past
and which made recommendations in a variety of areas, including health.
Dr. Nell Wyman was Canada's first female Aboriginal psychiatrist
and is based at McMaster University in Ontario.
And Nell is working to implement some of these calls to action from the commission.
Nell is in Melbourne for the Leaders in Indigenous Medical Education Conference.
Welcome to The Health Report.
Thank you, Norman. It's wonderful to be here.
And you're going out in Canada through CBC Radio.
I think it goes to air at some ungodly hour at half past four in the morning.
That's terrific.
So now, just briefly, tell us what these calls to action were in the health area in Canada from the Stolen Generation, although you don't call it that in Canada.
Right. So when the Truth and Reconciliation finally finished its seven-year process, they came out with 94 separate calls to action that were grouped into various themes.

And the health group includes seven specific calls to action, but the basic themes amongst those seven are, for example, increasing the number of Indigenous health professionals to work with our own people.
And that would be health professionals in a variety of disciplines, including medicine, nursing, occupational therapy, etc.

The second theme was centered around the recognition of the value of traditional healing practices and making those practices available to Indigenous people as part of accessing health care in general.

And the third theme centered around academic institutions like universities, places that train health professionals, not just Indigenous health professionals, but all health professionals, that they receive mandatory training as part of integrated into the curriculum that they receive during their education on Indigenous issues in general, the history of Indigenous people in Canada, and specific issues around Indigenous health.
and social determinants and cultural determinants of health.
What, I mean, when global issues around Indigenous peoples,
First Nations, as you call them in Canada, are discussed,
it's always said that the Australian Aboriginal people
are in the worst situation.
New Zealanders, Maori are better off,
and Canadian First Nations are better off,
both of which have, because they have treaties
and are better recognized by their countries.
But reading through some of the Truth and Reconciliation Commission,
it's not a great story.
No, it's not a great story.
But I think the process that we went through with the TRC in Canada
was very important.
And I think one of the things that really needs to happen,
not just in the health sphere and those of us who work with Indigenous people
in health context, but for the general Canadian population
and the world to realize that this process happened and why it's happening.
I think if you ask the average Canadian on the street,
they may not even know that we actually went through a process of speaking our truth
and coming up with these calls to action.
So that's one thing that Canada can do a lot better at.
The academic institutions, on the other hand, I think are feeling a bit of pressure now
to act upon these calls.
And that's why I think there's been a lot more attention paid to it
over the last year or so.
So what's happening at McMaster, which is known as a sort of frontline,
more innovative medical school than some of the others in Canada?
Right.
So McMaster University has a reputation for social responsibility,
social accountability.
But in terms of, for example, if we look at the calls to action
around curriculum, that's something that we've just started to address. So in fact, the trainees
at McMaster University in, for example, the medical school receive actually very little
exposure to indigenous health issues at present. But we're hoping to increase that now that we have
kind of the momentum of the truth and reconciliation behind us. So this is things like cultural
awareness training and so on? Yes, for example. I mean, the McMaster University, I mean, every
medical school now in Canada admits a very diverse class, right? So some of those, some of the
students may not be even that aware of Indigenous health issues. And that's why it's important to
include it as part of the regular curriculum and not just offer it, say, on an elective basis.
And are there quotas for First Nation candidates?
No, it really varies from school to school. But at McMaster University, we have what's called a
facilitated admissions process. So if someone meets the basic academic standards that all students
have to meet, then the program that I work in, which is the Indigenous Students Health Sciences
Program, we are able to provide support to those students as they go through the admissions process.
And we can recommend whether they are offered admission to the medical school or not.
but it has to be very clear to all the students that everyone starts at the same point.
They meet the same academic criteria that any other student has to meet.
So nothing patronizing.
Yes.
And just finally, I mean, the assumption is,
and the assumption is when you don't think about it too hard as well,
you know, an Aboriginal kid will come into medical school in Australia
and they'll go and work in an Aboriginal medical service.
But, you know, why shouldn't they, like you, become a psychiatrist or an obstetrician
or what have you?
It's just having more Indigenous people in the healthcare system in general.
Do you share that attitude?
Yeah, I do, actually.
I mean, I think for myself, as one of the first Aboriginal psychiatrists in Canada,
is mental health issues are actually very predominant on the needs of Indigenous people in my country
and as well as Australia, I imagine.
But I really do think it's important as an Indigenous physician
that we should be able to work wherever we want to across the country
bearing in mind that Indigenous people live in all sorts of settings across the country.
We're not just confined to small remote communities in the north.
In fact, more than half of Indigenous people in Canada live in urban centres.
Nell, thank you very much for joining us.
Thank you very much for having me and it's a pleasure to visit Australia.
Nell Wyman works at McMaster University in Hamilton, Ontario.
I'm Norman Swan and this has been The Health Report.
See you next time.
